assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Complementary base pairing
items.clue: A always joins with T, and G with C.

items.label: Template strand
items.clue: Its sequence directs the assembly of a new chain.

items.label: Double helix
items.clue: Two polynucleotide strands wound around each other.

items.label: Base sequence
items.clue: The order of nitrogenous bases along a nucleic acid strand.

questions.stem: Which statement about the genetic material of organisms is correct?

options.text: Every living organism, from bacteria to humans, uses DNA as its genetic material.
Some living organisms use RNA in place of DNA as their genetic material.
Genetic information in cells is stored in proteins rather than in DNA.
Living organisms vary in whether their genes are made of DNA or RNA.

questions.explanation: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms. The only entities that use RNA as genetic material are certain viruses, and viruses are not considered to be living.

questions.stem: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?

options.text: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.

questions.explanation: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.

questions.stem: What links one nucleotide to the next within a single strand of DNA?

options.text: A hydrogen bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
A covalent bond between the base of one nucleotide and the base of the next one.
A bond formed by adding water between the sugar of one nucleotide and the next.
A covalent bond from the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next.

questions.explanation: Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms along the strand, forming the strong backbone of the molecule.

questions.stem: Which list names the nitrogenous bases found in DNA?

options.text: Adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil.
Alanine, cysteine, glycine and threonine: four bases.

questions.explanation: DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the strand forms the basis of the genetic code.

questions.stem: How is a molecule of RNA formed from nucleotides?

options.text: Hydrolysis reactions join nucleotides through their sugars and phosphates, taking in a water molecule each time.
Hydrogen bonds form between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next in the chain.
Condensation reactions bond the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, releasing water.
Condensation reactions bond the base of one nucleotide to the base of the next, releasing water.

questions.explanation: RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers. Each condensation forms a covalent sugar–phosphate bond and releases one molecule of water.

questions.stem: The influenza virus contains RNA and no DNA. Why does this not contradict the statement that DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms?

options.text: The statement is a generalization, and influenza is one of its known exceptions.
Viruses are not considered to be living, so the statement does not apply to them.
The virus's RNA is not genetic material; its protein coat carries the genes.
RNA is just a single strand of DNA, so the virus's genetic material still counts as DNA.

questions.stem: A short RNA molecule is made by joining 20 nucleotides into a single strand. What happens to water during its formation?

options.text: 20 molecules of water are released, one for each nucleotide.
19 molecules of water are taken in, one to form each bond.
No water is involved, because the bonds are hydrogen bonds.
19 molecules of water are released, one per bond formed.

questions.explanation: Joining 20 nucleotides into one strand requires 19 sugar–phosphate bonds, and each bond is formed by a condensation reaction that releases one molecule of water: 19 in total.
